title: Origami Sampler: latency-cost annotated draft
summary: Working draft benchmark tracing how an "origami" sampling policy transitions microburst traffic to sustained handling across model variants; focuses on p50/p90/p99 latency and dollars-per-1000-requests for three knobs (tiling, kv-prefetch, quant profile). Includes compact ASCII charts and recommended next steps for console UI metrics.
content:
Purpose
This doc captures a small targeted benchmark run we did to explore the latency/cost tradeoffs of a lightweight sampling policy we call 'origami sampler' — it selectively samples microburst requests into a fast-path (small-batch, minimal prefetch) versus a sustained-path (tiling + aggressive kv-prefetch + quant profile). The goal is to find operating points where p90/p99 costs are reduced without regressively harming p50 for interactive flows.

Test rig and methodology
- Date: runs between 2028-03-10 and 2028-03-12.
- Hardware: dedicated cluster c5x-large (4xA100-sim nodes) in region us-central.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime v5.2 with dynamic-tiling patch ORIGAMI-3.
- Models: small-chat (7B fp16), small-chat-quant (7B int8 profile q2), and medium-chat (13B fp16).
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes derived from production session traces: (A) spike-heavy microburst (90% short-chat, 10% long), (B) steady sustained (median tokens 120), (C) mixed diurnal pattern.
- Traffic shape: burst windows of 1–5s with peak qps 600; baseline sustained 40 qps.
- Measurement: token-latency end-to-end (client->response), token cost estimated via runtime token accounting. 95% CI from 5 repeated runs.

Sampling policy knobs evaluated
1) Fast-path threshold: requests with instantaneous qps delta > 80% go to fast-path.
2) Fast-path config: small-batch size 8, no kv-prefetch, FP16 kernels.
3) Sustained-path config: tiling enabled, batch size 64, kv-prefetch on, quant profile Q2 enabled for small-chat-quant.
4) Graceful-handoff window: 2s, 5s tested.

Key observed metrics (aggregated)
- Metric abbreviations: p50/p90/p99 in ms, cost in USD per 1k requests.

Table: aggregate snapshot (workload A microburst)
Model        | Path      | p50  | p90  | p99  | cost/1k
--------------------------------------------------
small-chat   | fast      | 28ms | 75ms | 210ms| $0.86
small-chat   | sustained | 36ms | 110ms| 420ms| $0.54
small-chat-q | sustained | 42ms | 150ms| 630ms| $0.32
medium-chat  | sustained | 88ms | 260ms| 900ms| $1.45

Interpretation of table
- Fast-path reduces p50 substantially for small-chat at the expense of higher per-request cost — small batches have worse amortization but cut p50 and p90 during spikes.
- Quantized sustained variants have lower cost per 1k requests but p99 stretches, particularly under burst-induced contention.

ASCII heatmap: p90 latency (ms) vs QPS and Tiling ON/OFF (workload A)
QPS ->  50    100    200    400    600
TILING=OFF  45    62     95    180    300
TILING=ON   48    58     78    120    160
(Interpretation: tiling benefits become pronounced beyond 200 qps; tiling reduces p90 slope and compresses tail.)

Microburst cost curve (approx dollars per 1k) — small-chat fast vs sustained (sparklines)
fast-path : $0.86 | ▁▂▆▇▇
sustained  : $0.54 | ▁▃▄▅▆
quant-sust  : $0.32 | ▁▁▂▃▅
(Explanation: sparkline left-to-right represents rising instantaneous qps within a burst window; fast-path cost growth is steeper because small batches are used to preserve latency.)

Tradeoff map (text)
- If product requires p50 < 35ms during spikes: enable origami sampler with fast-path fraction up to 35% of requests during a burst; accept 35–60% increase in dollars/1k for those windows.
- If unit cost is critical and p99 < 500ms acceptable: prefer quantized sustained path with tiling and longer handoff window (5s). This reduces cost/1k by ~40% compared to fast-path.
- Handoff sensitivity: short handoff (2s) keeps more requests on fast-path and reduces p50 but increases cost; longer handoff yields smoother amortization.

Operational notes for console metrics
- We need two new charts in the runtime console: 1) 'burst-mode split' showing fraction of requests routed fast vs sustained over time, 2) 'hand-off latency delta' showing moving p50/p90 difference between paths. Both should be available at tenant and model level.
- Alerting: add a percentile-based alert when >20% of requests are routed fast-path for >30s at sustained qps > 200. This indicates potential under-provisioning or mis-configured handoff.

Gotchas and anomalies seen
- We observed occasional p99 spikes on quant-profile sustained-path when mixed with medium-chat concurrently — suspected GPU memory fragmentation during tiling transitions. Reproducible when mixed-model concurrency > 1.2x baseline.
- Warm-up penalty: switching a tile group from idle to active had a 60–120ms penalty once every ~300s; this contributed to the p99 in steady runs. Consider soft-prewarm heuristics.

Recommended next experiments
1) A/B run with adaptive batch sizing: let sustained-path auto-shrink batch size during tail-end of bursts to see if p99 drop can be achieved while keeping cost low.
2) Memory-pressure microbench: exercise mixed-model tiling transitions at controlled concurrency to confirm fragmentation hypothesis.
3) Uniform quant ladder test: test q2 vs q3 profiles under same workload to measure quality vs tail.
4) Real-user pilot: enable origami sampler for 5% of production traffic for 48 hours with detailed tracing.

Quick checklist for featureization
- [ ] Console charts: burst-mode split, hand-off delta.
- [ ] Runtime knobs: graceful-handoff window, fast-path batch size, quant preference per-tenant.
- [ ] Metrics: cost/1k estimation per path, per-model; path-conversion rate during bursts.

Appendix: short raw sample of a single-run timeline (ms) for small-chat, QPS trace and p90 series
Time(s):    0   1   2   3   4   5   6
QPS:        40  100 240 580 400 120 45
p90-fast:   40  70  90  110 95  68  46
p90-sust:   48  70  115 180 140 86  50
(Shows handoff window effect: at t=3 the fast-path holds lower p90 while sustained climbs sharply; after 5s sustained amortizes and p90 falls.)

Notes to reviewers
- This is a working draft intended to capture the shape of tradeoffs, not exhaustive. Numbers are rough-aggregates from a few runs. Please flag any outlier behavior you want instrumented for further drilldowns.
- If approved, I'll convert this into a short PRD for the console changes and open the origami sampler experiment as a runtime feature-flagged rollout.

Acknowledgements
Thanks to Marcus for running the traces and Diego for the cost-accounting helpers. Priya contributed the handoff heuristics prototype.
